title: Banana peels for Krishna
hookLine: Krishna turns down a palace feast and eats at a humble house, where he's handed the peels
carry: bhava: god takes the feeling, not the finish

lines: A FEAST TO WIN KRISHNA OVER.
cards: Remember day seventy-five: Krishna in Hastinapura, asking for peace. Duryodhana has laid out a feast to win him over, gold plates, every dish the palace kitchens can make. Krishna says no.
In the Mahabharata he puts it plainly: people eat at someone's table out of love, or out of need, and here there's neither.
Then he walks across the city to the small house of Vidura, the old king's wise, humble half-brother. Nobody there is expecting God for dinner.

teach.b: Families love to tell what happened next, in a telling sung in devotional songs more than written in the epic. Vidura's wife is home when Krishna walks in, and she's so overjoyed she can't think straight.

teach.h: NOT AS SWEET AS THE PEELS.
teach.b: She sits him down, grabs some bananas, peels them, and in her excitement throws the fruit aside and hands him the peels. And Krishna eats them, one after another, smiling, as if he's never tasted anything better.
When Vidura gets home he's horrified, and serves the fruit properly. Krishna takes a bite and says, gently, it isn't as sweet as the peels.

teach.h: BHAVA: THE FEELING INSIDE THE OFFERING.
teach.b: That's the teaching, and it has a name: bhava, the feeling inside an offering.
An old Sanskrit saying makes the same point with a grammar joke: one person says Vishnu's name with the ending wrong, a scholar says it right, and both earn the same, because God takes the feeling.
It's why Hindus worship the way they do.

teach.h: MURTI: A FORM GOD IS INVITED INTO.
teach.b: Today's word, murti, is a form God is invited into. A temple murti may be carved by trained hands, but in many pujas Ganesha is first called into a little cone of turmeric paste, or a single betel nut. No trunk, no ears.
Shiva is honored as a smooth stone. Now, a kitchen table, the week before Ganesh Chaturthi. Someone has made a clay Ganesha for the family shrine.
The trunk leans; one ear is bigger. Next to the perfect ones online it looks clumsy, and the worry comes: am I doing this wrong? Krishna ate the peels.

teach.h: GOD TAKES THE FEELING, NOT THE FINISH.
teach.b: The feeling is the offering; the clay carries it.

how: Many families bring home or make a clay Ganesha for Ganesh Chaturthi, often of natural clay so it dissolves at the immersion; in many pujas Ganesha is first invoked in a small cone of turmeric paste or a betel nut. Devotional songs retell Krishna eating at Vidura's house.

s: Krishna ate at Duryodhana's palace feast
he refused it: no love, no need. he ate at Vidura's humble house instead.
a murti has to be perfectly made to be worshiped
in many pujas Ganesha is first called into a cone of turmeric or a betel nut. the feeling is what's offered.
an old Sanskrit saying: God takes the feeling, even when the grammar's wrong
bhava, the feeling inside an offering, counts more than getting every detail right.

games.q: your homemade clay Ganesha is lopsided. your cousin's, from the shop, is perfect. the festival starts tonight. what do you do?
o: hide yours and borrow your cousin's.
welcome yours home, trunk and all.
skip this year and practice for next year.
games.why: Krishna ate the peels at Vidura's house and smiled. bhava, the feeling inside the offering, is what God takes, so the lopsided one made with love is welcome.

practice: This is the oldest offering there is. Pick one small thing you can give: a flower, a piece of fruit, a spoon of something you cooked, or just a glass of water.
Notice the voice that says it isn't enough, not fancy, not done right; let it talk. Then picture Vidura's wife, so happy she handed God the peels, and Krishna smiling as he ate.
If you have a shrine or a picture of God at home, set your offering before it with both hands, the way families offer food before a meal, and say a name you love, Krishna or Ganesha, once.
If you don't pray, set it down for someone you love, a parent or a friend, and give it with your whole heart. Either way, the gift is the feeling. Stay with that for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Murti. A form, a body: the shape God is invited into, from carved stone to a cone of turmeric, honored for the love inside it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a form, a body, an embodiment. the figure in which the divine is honored.

carryVoice: Your line: bhava, God takes the feeling, not the finish. Krishna ate the peels. On to day eighty-seven.
